name: Klein Epley Qualify Reduced Over Approval Through Group Lie Detection
text: Klein and Epley qualify Kaal's exploratory over-approval result with four experiments on human lie detection. Three-person groups that discussed their judgments distinguished truths from lies more accurately than individuals. The gain came primarily from identifying lies correctly, not from improved truth detection or a change in the tendency to answer 'lie.' Statistical aggregation of individual answers did not reproduce the effect. The source therefore supports a narrow mechanism correspondence: discussion can reduce acceptance of false content through information created in interaction. The comparison remains limited. The experiments concern human judgments about deceptive statements. They do not test multi-model validation pools, ground-truth work approval, unanimity, or Kaal's reported effect sizes.

Correctly identifying a lie is analogous only to rejecting false content. It is not the same operational measure as Kaal's ground-truth over-approval endpoint.

sourceProvenance.sourceProposition: Across four experiments, Klein and Epley found that three-person discussion improved lie detection mainly by increasing correct identification of lies rather than truths, and that the advantage arose from discussion rather than opinion aggregation or response bias.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: In four experiments, we find that groups are consistently more accurate than individuals in distinguishing truths from lies, an effect that comes primarily from an increased ability to correctly identify when a person is lying.

As Table 1 shows, the group advantage came primarily from detecting lies more accurately than individuals [t(118) = 2.80, P < 0.01, d = 0.57, 95% CIdifference, 3.7%, 21.6%]. There was no group advantage when detecting truths [t(118) = 0.73, P = 0.47, d = 0.13, 95% CIdifference, -6.1%, 13.1%].

This group advantage in lie detection did not come through the statistical aggregation of individual opinions as often shown in existing research (a wisdom-of-crowds effect), but instead through the process of group discussion.
